title: Nutrition in Humans
seo_title: Secondary 3 Biology: Nutrition in Humans Worksheets (O-Level 6093 with Answers)
standard_text: Describe the functions of the main parts of the alimentary canal and associated organs in ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion; describe mechanical and chemical digestion, including the roles of amylase, maltase, proteases and lipase and of bile in emulsifying fats; describe the structure of a villus and how it is adapted for absorption; describe the hepatic portal vein and the roles of the liver in carbohydrate metabolism, deamination and the breakdown of alcohol (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Biology 6093 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 3 O-Level Biology worksheets on nutrition in humans: the alimentary canal, digestive enzymes, bile, villi and absorption, and the liver. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Big insoluble molecules → small soluble ones.
key_sub: Absorbed in the ileum, sent to the liver by the hepatic portal vein.
body_html:
How to think about it

Food passes mouth → oesophagus → stomach → duodenum → ileum → colon → rectum.

  • Starch → maltose (amylase) → glucose (maltase). Protein → polypeptides (pepsin, trypsin) → amino acids (peptidase). Fat → fatty acids + glycerol (lipase).
  • Bile, made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder, emulsifies fat. It is not an enzyme.
  • Villi give a huge surface area, thin walls, capillaries and lacteals for absorption.
  • The liver stores glycogen, deaminates excess amino acids to urea and breaks down alcohol.
Example

Enzyme for maltose → glucose?

maltose is the substrate

Answer: maltase

Example

Why many villi?

villi increase surface area

Answer: faster absorption

Common mistakes

  • Calling bile an enzyme.
  • Saying protein digestion starts in the mouth.
  • Saying most absorption happens in the stomach or colon.
  • Saying villi increase the volume rather than the surface area.

faq.q: What is the difference between digestion and absorption?
faq.a: Digestion breaks large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble ones. Absorption is the movement of these small molecules through the wall of the small intestine into the blood or lymph.

faq.q: How is a villus adapted for absorption?
faq.a: It has microvilli for a large surface area, a wall one cell thick, a rich supply of capillaries to keep a steep gradient and a lacteal to absorb fats.

faq.q: What does the liver do with excess amino acids?
faq.a: It deaminates them: the amino group is removed and converted to urea, which is excreted by the kidneys; the rest can be used for energy.
